findings.message: A different agent (Claude) checked the work in a separate headless process.

I found no blocking errors, so I'm approving with five warnings. The feature has 12 scenario blocks that compile to 17 cases, which matches the ticket's work log and dimensions.md. Every Rule (R1–R5) in spec.md has acceptance coverage. Each spec obligation not covered by an acceptance scenario is assigned to a named lower-level matrix in dimensions.md: wrong-purpose and unauthenticated records, duplicate or ambiguous results, dirty input at verification time, unchanged-content commits, and in-place input changes during a run. I cross-checked the counts in the supplied material and they agree: 11 mapped proof files, 37 cases across the 14 blocks in proof-map.md, and 33 deferrals split DRD65E 1, KKP2R3 2, MCWV4B 18, FC33HK 12. The scenarios include passing controls next to the refusal cases: the demo success and the Work Log and audit-only rows that keep currency. Several feasibility points remain implementation-planning obligations and are explicitly recorded as such.

The @demo scenario assumes that all 37 T3E4NS cases can be mapped to passing named assertions. proof-map.md's 'Certification gap' section and the work log both leave mapping feasibility open. Examples are the fallback order across both declaration orders and the route-admission partitions, where the degraded-labeling test is only supporting evidence. If any case is honestly unsupported, R2 requires a named refusal, and the killer demo cannot pass without weakening a case. Settle feasibility before implementation, or expect the demo's Given to fail rather than adjusting it.

The 'unmapped delivery case' scenario needs a fixture whose shipped contract lacks one of the 37 mappings. R1 and the observer-shipped-profile matrix say a committed project edit cannot shrink the installed required set. Implementation planning must say how that fixture is built through a real alternative shipped contract rather than a project or caller edit. Otherwise the test either proves nothing or opens the census-override path that R1 forbids.

The mid-run candidate scenario can be read two ways. An observer running in an isolated checkout pinned to commit X could treat the original checkout advancing as irrelevant. Or it could compare the original HEAD at the end of the run. Only the second meets the scenario as written. The work log already lists this as an open planning obligation. Make sure the plan says which reference is compared, and that the in-place lockfile/config change inside the isolated tree is covered by observer-source-identity, so the scenario does not pass without detecting a real input change.

R5's spec text requires that refused observations also carry the execution-evidence-only meaning and change no historical or closing authority. The acceptance scenario only covers the successful path. dimensions.md moves the refused and interrupted paths to observer-history-preservation and observer-recovery-messages. That placement is acceptable, but those matrices must actually assert the meaning label and byte-identical history on the refusal paths.

The R4 outline covers only committed changes. Spec R4 also covers dirty inputs and new commits with unchanged content at verification time, and these rely solely on observer-freshness. Keep the whole-ticket-exemption and whole-ticket-hash mutations named in dimensions.md. They are the only discriminating controls showing that the Work Log 'current' row is not met by exempting the whole ticket.md.
